title: Learning about the moa

paragraphs.text: In 1839, John W Harris, a New Zealand trader who was a natural history enthusiast, was given a piece of unusual bone by someone who had found it in a river bank. This bone, a piece of femur, ended up in England in the hands of Professor Richard Owen, a leading biologist and palaeontologist. After careful examination of the bone, Owen made his pronouncement in 1840: ‘there had existed and perhaps still exists in New Zealand a race of ... birds of larger and more colossal size than the ostrich or any known species.’ This deduction was made from a mere fragment of a femur some six inches in length.

A hundred years later, in 1939, a schoolboy, Jim Eyles, discovered a Maori* burial site at the Wairau Bar, on the north-eastern shore of New Zealand’s South Island, containing tools and ornaments and a complete moa egg. Further evidence suggests that these Maori hunted and herded moa, probably with the help of dogs, along the eight-kilometre-long gravel bar to an encampment at the bar’s end.

Subsequent investigations showed that early Maori, some 600 years ago, utilised moa for a variety of purposes. They fashioned jewellery as well as fish hooks and harpoon heads from the large bones, while the skins and feathers were used for clothing. Besides being eaten, the eggs were emptied and used as water containers. When Europeans arrived, there were so many moa bones around in some areas that they crushed them for fertiliser.

Moa had large legs and no wings at all. This was a unique feature among birds, and meant that the moa had no real breast muscles. Based on what could be learnt from feathers that have been found, they were reddish brown birds with feathers perhaps tipped with white and black. Some of the feathers found have a yellowish central stripe. Moa were very long birds, not tall birds as the early depictions would have them. Contrary to the way it was initially represented in paintings and drawings, the moa head was actually held only slightly above the level of the back. Females were huge, standing at nearly two metres high. There seems to have been a very pronounced degree of difference between genders, with females being up to 150% as tall and 280% as heavy as males. Such was the difference in stature that until 2003 females were classified as separate species.

Questions have been asked about how the moa arrived in New Zealand. They may have already been in New Zealand as it broke away from Antarctica 70 million years ago. At that time, Antarctica, as evidenced by plant fossils, was subtropical and supported an environment lush with vegetation. Richard Dawkins, the British biologist, suggests that Antarctica provided a ‘land bridge linking Africa and South America on one side of the world to Australia and New Zealand on the other’.

The idea, starting with early writers such as Julius von Haast, a geologist and surveyor of New Zealand, that moa were grassland grazing birds, prevailed until the 1980s when research concluded that moa were forest birds. The moa’s bill structure, gizzard stones and gizzard contents, all suggest that the great birds favoured a very fibrous diet dominated by twigs, snipped by their specially adapted beaks from low trees and shrubs.

The lifespan of the moa and most features of its biology are matters for speculation. However, large birds generally live a long time, perhaps 50 years or so, given the lack of predators. Moa were a typical example of a ‘K-adapted species’** which produce small numbers of young, have a long gestation and generally have a lack of defensive or escape capability.

Moa may have been hunted to extinction two hundred years after humans first arrived in New Zealand. They made such easy prey that by 1200 the hunting of moa alone provided food surpluses sufficient to enable the settling of large villages. These villages were permanent coastal encampments from which bands would set out to hunt and carry back moa. With such abundance came a good deal of waste; as much as 50% of usable weight was discarded in the field. However, by the late 1400s, the moa hunting society had collapsed, as the supply had been over-exploited. By about 1400, when moa are generally thought to have become extinct, the Haast’s Eagle, which had relied on moa for food, had also become extinct, probably as a result of diminished food supply.

The nearest relatives of the moa were once considered to be the kiwi, but research published in 2005 comparing their DNA suggested the moa were more closely related to the Australian emu and cassowary. More recently, research published in 2010 found that the moa’s DNA is more similar to smaller terrestrial South American birds called the tinamous than it is to that of the emu and cassowary. It is likely that the moa will continue to be a source of fascination to researchers.

subtitle: Most species of moa, a bird that was unique to New Zealand, had become extinct by around the year 1400
footnotes: * Maori: people who first arrived in New Zealand in the thirteenth century
** K-adapted species: a category of animals that have relatively stable populations and produce low numbers of offspring
